newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Union demonstration blocks traffic in EU district.
newsitem.headline: Union demonstration blocks traffic in EU district.

text.p: Thousands of workers demanding more European Union action to fight record unemployment brought traffic to a temporary standstill in Brussels' EU quarter on Wednesday, forming a human chain between the bloc's buildings.
Clad in the blue, yellow and red vests of Belgian unions, the demonstrators carried banners urging EU leaders to create a "social Europe". They threw firecrackers, chanted and danced.
A union spokesman estimated the number at more than 10,000.
"We are showing solidarity with all the unemployed," Anne-Marie Celander, a Swedish graphic worker, told Reuters.
She was part of a group of 25 unemployed Swedes who had travelled to Brussels to take part in the demonstration, which coincided with similar workers' events in more than 20 European countries.
The European Trade Union confederation (ETUC) called the "European Day of Action for Employment" with further rallies scheduled across the continent from Belgium to Bulgaria.
It urged EU leaders meeting in Amsterdam on June 16-17 to lay the foundations for a social Europe "which puts economic and employment policies on par with monetary policies."
The Amsterdam meeting is expected to agree a new EU treaty, including a chapter on the fight against unemployment.
The action day followed worker rallies in western Europe in recent months against factory closures and industry-restructuring as companies respond to intensifying competition.
The announcement in February by French car maker Renault of plans to shut down its Vilvoorde plant near Brussels with the loss of 3,100 jobs sparked angry demonstrations.

"The recent industrial conflicts across Europe clearly have shown that people will have nothing to do with a union which disregards their legitimate employment and social policy aspirations," ETUC said in a statement this week.
Despite EU declarations about the need to bring down unemployment, the EU jobless rate remained at 10.9 percent in March, which meant 18.3 million people in the 15-nation union were out of work.
